family_1_ubs_literally_hence.question: The source often gives the Hebrew word for word and then what that wording means, inside one text, like: literally: to dig (an area); hence: = action by which ... Should the word-for-word wording and what it means be two readings? A proper name or a title with its description, a wording that itself says how it turns to the meaning or that holds a description, a short gloss written with the sign >, and a text whose brackets do not pair stay as one reading under either answer. A text that opens with a label, or whose wording says in what kind of text it is found, has its own question, B04.

options.means: The page prints the wording as one reading and what it means as another, with any lead word of the source's own and the notes that follow it: literally: to dig (an area), and hence: = action by which ... Where a text takes two such steps, each step is its own reading.
The page keeps the wording and what it means together in one reading, as the source writes it.
